---
title: "ConvolutionInterpolations.jl"
subtitle: "The reference implementation, in Julia"
engine: julia
---

ConvolutionInterpolations.jl is the package in which the convolution kernels were developed, and
it has every capability described on this site: interpolation, differentiation, integration and
smoothing on uniform grids, interpolation on nonuniform grids, resampling, and fitting to
scattered data, in any number of dimensions. It is registered in the Julia General registry.

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
using ConvolutionInterpolations
println("This site was rendered against version ", pkgversion(ConvolutionInterpolations), ".")
```

## Installation

```julia
using Pkg
Pkg.add("ConvolutionInterpolations")
```

The package depends only on the standard library and a handful of small registered packages;
plotting is not among them, so the examples on this site load `Plots` separately.

## The functions

Everything is reached through six exported functions, each returning an interpolant that is
called like a function:

| Function | What it does | Concept page |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `convolution_interpolation(knots, data)` | Interpolates gridded data, uniform or not, with derivatives and integrals by keyword | [Interpolation](../concepts/interpolation.qmd), [Derivatives](../concepts/derivatives.qmd), [Integrals](../concepts/integrals.qmd), [Nonuniform grids](../concepts/nonuniform.qmd) |
| `convolution_interpolation(points, values)` | Fits a grid to scattered points, smoothing noisy data or interpolating trusted data exactly | [Scattered data](../concepts/scattered.qmd) |
| `fit_scattered(points, values)` | The fit behind the scattered-data method, returning the fitted grid itself | [Scattered data](../concepts/scattered.qmd) |
| `convolution_smooth(knots, data, B)` | Gaussian smoothing of gridded data, separably in any dimension | [Smoothing](../concepts/smoothing.qmd) |
| `convolution_gaussian(knots, data, B)` | The same smoothing as an interpolant, evaluated anywhere | [Smoothing](../concepts/smoothing.qmd) |
| `convolution_resample(knots, data, new_knots)` | Resamples from one uniform grid to another, optionally differentiating in the same pass | [Interpolation](../concepts/interpolation.qmd) |

The kernels themselves are selected with the `kernel` keyword, `:a0` to `:a7` and `:b5` to `:b13`
on uniform grids and `:n3` or `:b5` to `:b13` on nonuniform ones; the
[interpolation page](../concepts/interpolation.qmd) has the table of their degrees, continuity
and convergence orders, and the [API reference](api.qmd) has every keyword.

## What is specific to Julia

The Python port reproduces the numerics of this package to the last bit, so the differences are
in what the language allows rather than in the results:

- **Generic element types.** The interpolants work for any floating-point type: `Float32` for
  memory, `Float64` as the default, `BigFloat` for arbitrary precision. The kernel polynomials
  are derived in exact rational arithmetic and rounded once to the working precision, so a
  `BigFloat` interpolant is accurate to that precision, not to `Float64`.
- **Allocation-free evaluation.** Evaluating an interpolant allocates nothing, and the cost of a
  uniform-grid evaluation does not depend on the grid size. Interpolants can be evaluated from
  several threads at once.
- **Lazy construction for large grids.** Boundary ghost values are normally precomputed when the
  interpolant is built; for large grids in several dimensions the package instead computes them
  on the fly in boundary cells (`lazy=true`), so construction takes about a millisecond whatever
  the grid, and no enlarged copy of the data is made. The default chooses by the size of the grid.
- **Extrapolation.** The `extrap` keyword chooses what happens outside the data: `:throw`
  (the default), `:flat`, `:line` or `:natural`. The Python port does not extrapolate yet.
- **Nonuniform grids are detected.** Passing nonuniformly spaced knots switches to the
  nonuniform kernels without any keyword; the [nonuniform page](../concepts/nonuniform.qmd)
  explains what changes.
- **Plotting.** The examples on this site use `Plots`; the interpolants broadcast like any Julia
  function, so `itp.(xs)` and `itp.(xs, ys')` are all that is needed for lines and surfaces.
